title: A coin in a fish (Matthew 17:14–27)
hookLine: free, and paying anyway: a tax, a fish, and faith the size of a seed
tomorrow: the disciples ask who's the greatest. why does he call over a child?

cards: Anyone who has paid a fee they were pretty sure they didn't owe, just to stop an argument, will recognize this scene. In Capernaum, the men who collect the temple tax stop Peter: "Doth not your master pay tribute?"
Peter says yes, fast, the way you answer at a door. Inside, Jesus asks him a question. Kings collect from strangers, or from their own children?
Strangers, Peter says. "Then are the children free." So Jesus doesn't owe it.
And he pays anyway. With a coin from a fish's mouth. Why?

teach.b: Start with his reason, which Matthew gives in four words: "lest we should offend them." He's free, and he pays, so that nobody stumbles over a small thing. Then the odd part.

teach.h: CAST A HOOK, OPEN ITS MOUTH.
teach.b: Go to the sea, he tells Peter, cast a hook, take the first fish that comes up, open its mouth, and you'll find a piece of money. "That take, and give unto them for me and thee."
He sends a fisherman to do the one thing he already knows how to do.

Here's something to tell a friend tonight: Matthew never says Peter caught the fish. The chapter ends on the instruction. Earlier that same chapter, the disciples had failed to heal a boy and asked why.

teach.h: FAITH AS A GRAIN OF MUSTARD SEED.
teach.b: Jesus answered, because of your unbelief, and then: "If ye have faith as a grain of mustard seed, ye shall say unto this mountain, Remove hence to yonder place; and it shall remove." So that's the puzzle solved.
Not a mountain of faith. A seed of it. One coin, one cast line, one small trust, enough to cover a debt for two.
The big things in this chapter keep turning out small.

how: Christians often quote the mustard seed line when someone feels their faith is too small, and some read Matthew 17 as a picture of paying what's asked even when you could argue it.

games.q: what does “a coin in a fish” mean?
o: a tax Jesus didn't owe, paid from a fish's mouth
a miracle that fed a crowd from one fish
a parable about saving money for hard times

games.q: the tax and the seed — tap the pairs.
p: doth not your master pay tribute?
a piece of money in its mouth
the faith that moves a mountain

s: Jesus said you need huge faith to move a mountain
faith as a grain of mustard seed: the size he names is tiny.
Matthew describes Peter catching the fish and finding the coin
the chapter ends on the instruction. the catch is never shown.
Jesus said the children are free, and paid anyway
lest we should offend them: free, and paying, so no one stumbles.

games.q: your friend says you owe four dollars for snacks. you're fairly sure you don't, and she's getting annoyed. what does the fish story point toward?
o: pay it, without a fuss, so a small thing doesn't become a big one.
prove you're right first; Jesus said the children are free.
pay it, but tell everyone you never actually owed it.
games.why: Jesus says the children are free, and pays anyway, lest we should offend them. being right and paying aren't opposites.

practice: Bring to mind one small thing you owe: a few dollars, a borrowed book, a thank-you you never sent. If you can settle it from where you're sitting, do it now, quickly and without a fuss; if not, decide exactly when.
Small is enough here. That was the whole point of the seed.

wordCard.voice: A coin in a fish. A tax Jesus didn't owe, paid anyway, from the first fish on Peter's hook.

orig.note: Greek: the tax coin the collectors ask about in Matthew 17:24; the King James says tribute.

carryVoice: Hold onto this one: faith moves mountains, and it starts the size of a seed. Until tomorrow.
